design_detail: Invited Comment in The Lancet (2018;392:987–88, issue of 22 September 2018, open access) published with the GBD 2016 alcohol paper (Griswold et al., 2018). Two authors; five paragraphs of running text and 14 references, one of them a review whose first author is R Burton. It restates GBD 2016's headline results, endorses its conclusions and argues for population-level alcohol policy (taxation and minimum unit pricing, marketing regulation, restricted availability). No methods, search or data of its own. Design 'narrative-review' with the editors' checklist, as the round brief directs for commentaries.
can_establish: How two clinicians and public-health researchers (King's College London, University of Southampton, both employed by Public Health England) read GBD 2016 on publication, and the arguments they gave for population-level alcohol policy.
cannot_establish: Anything about the health effects of alcohol beyond what GBD 2016 itself shows: every figure is second-hand from that paper; the title's statement that no level of consumption improves health is stronger than GBD 2016's own interval for the minimum-risk level (0 to 0.8 drinks a day); and the policy statements rest on one cited review rather than on any appraisal in the comment.

sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria; 14 references chosen by the authors.
sample.selection_effects: Selective by design. The two meta-analyses reporting lower mortality or cardiovascular risk at moderate intake (Ronksley et al., 2011; Di Castelnuovo et al., 2006) are cited only as the view GBD 2016 superseded; the critiques of that view (Fillmore et al., 2006; Britton & Bell, 2017; Naimi et al., 2017; Holmes et al., 2014; Stockwell et al., 2016) are cited as the emerging literature that allows more reliable estimates; the policy paragraph rests on a single review (Burton et al., 2017, an English perspective on alcohol control policies).

exposure.measurement: Not applicable; the comment restates GBD 2016's modelled exposure.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Restates the GBD 2016 minimum-risk level as 0 g of ethanol per week, without its interval (2nd paragraph).

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable (no data). The comment discusses alcohol-attributable deaths and DALYs as reported by GBD 2016, and harm beyond health (to families, through crime and disorder, in the workplace) and to people other than the drinker, without figures.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Improves health' is not defined; the comment equates it with GBD 2016's minimum of the DALY-weighted curve.

analysis.effect_sizes: None of its own. Restated from GBD 2016 and checked against that paper (card sc_griswold_2018): alcohol the seventh leading risk factor for deaths and DALYs in 2016; 2.2% (95% UI 1.5–3.0) of female and 6.8% (5.8–8.0) of male deaths; at ages 15–49, 3.8% (3.2–4.3) of female and 12.2% (10.8–13.6) of male deaths; minimum-risk level 0 g of ethanol a week.
analysis.selective_reporting: The comment leaves out GBD 2016's interval for the minimum (0 to 0.8 drinks a day in that paper's results), its statistically significant J-shaped curve for ischaemic heart disease, and its stated limitations other than unrecorded consumption and drinking patterns; it gives no figures for harm to others or for the effects of the policies it recommends.

interpretation_gap.results_show: GBD 2016 estimated that alcohol was the seventh leading risk factor worldwide and the leading one at ages 15–49, and that one globally DALY-weighted curve had its minimum at zero drinks a day with an interval reaching 0.8 drinks a day, while ischaemic heart disease showed a significant J-shaped association.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title states that no level of alcohol consumption improves health; the comment calls the analysis “state-of-the-art epidemiology” giving a “definitive understanding of alcohol-related harm” (3rd paragraph), calls its conclusions “clear and unambiguous” (4th paragraph), and takes them as strong support for the UK Chief Medical Officers' guideline, quoted as finding “no safe level of alcohol consumption”. Gaps: (1) a minimum of zero with an interval up to 0.8 drinks a day does not show that no level improves health, and the GBD authors later agreed that the risk is low across that range (authors' reply, 2019); (2) the minimum is described as minimising an individual's risk (2nd paragraph), though it comes from a curve weighted by the world population's disease mix; (3) 'definitive' is applied to a new method whose weighting four letters criticized in 2019 and whose global zero the same consortium revised to 0.511 drinks a day in 2022; (4) the policy paragraph mixes evidence (one cited review) with a prediction (that mortality in Scotland and England might diverge dramatically within a few years) and value statements (that limiting young people's exposure to marketing “has no downsides”; that these diseases are driven by commercial interests) without marking which is which.

timeline.event: Burton et al., rapid evidence review of the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of alcohol control policies from an English perspective (Lancet), the comment's source for its policy ranking; not read here.
GBD 2016 alcohol paper (Griswold et al.), the paper commented on: minimum-risk level zero (0–0.8) drinks a day (card sc_griswold_2018).

Four letters on GBD 2016 and the GBD authors' reply (Lancet 2019;393:2389–92; summarized on card sc_griswold_2018). Di Castelnuovo, Costanzo & de Gaetano cite this comment's title as the conclusion that cannot be drawn from GBD 2016; the GBD authors agree the risk is low between 0 and 0.8 drinks a day.
GBD 2020 (Bryazka et al.): global minimum-risk level 0.511 (0.400–0.700) drinks a day; minima between 0 and 0.603 at ages 15–39 and J-shaped weighted curves at 40 and older (card sc_bryazka_2022).

Burton & Sheron's comment on GBD 2020 (Lancet 2022;400:141–43; DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(22)01288-0): its first paragraph says the new findings seemingly contradict the 2018 message that any amount of alcohol leads to health loss; the rest is paywalled and was not read.
Controlled interrupted time-series evaluation of minimum unit pricing in Scotland (Wyper et al., 2023), on the project's Alcohol list, bears on the comment's prediction for Scotland; not read here.

replication.where_it_stands: A short endorsement written on publication. Its title states more than GBD 2016's own interval supports, and that paper's global minimum was revised to about half a drink a day by the same consortium in 2022, when the authors themselves described the new estimates as seemingly contradicting the earlier message. Cited for how the 'no safe level' reading was framed, not for any estimate.

funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: RB is employed full-time at Public Health England (PHE), is a visiting researcher at King's College London, and declares no other competing interests. NS is employed part-time at PHE; has received research grants from the British Liver Trust, the Alcohol Education Research Council and other funding bodies; has done paid consultancy and received travel expenses from Gilead; has been paid for medicolegal work on hepatitis C and alcohol-related liver disease; and is clinical adviser to PHE, scientific adviser to the European Public Health Alliance, and Royal College of Physicians representative on EU alcohol-policy bodies, the EU Alcohol Forum, the Alcohol Health Alliance UK, several UK government departments, NICE, Southampton City Council and liver and gastroenterology societies. One GBD 2016 author (F Greaves) is affiliated with PHE but had no involvement in or knowledge of the Comment.
funding.affiliations_note: Affiliations: Addictions Department, Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology & Neuroscience, King's College London (RB); Clinical Hepatology, Faculty of Medicine, University of Southampton (NS). Both authors were employed by Public Health England, a government agency; the cited policy review has R Burton as first author; no alcohol-industry ties are declared. Recorded as flags for closer reading, not as reasons to discount.

what_would_settle_it: For the health statement, the evidence named on cards sc_griswold_2018 and sc_bryazka_2022: low-intake dose–response curves from designs less exposed to confounding and abstainer bias, with a weighting scheme fixed in advance. For the policy prediction, controlled evaluations of minimum unit pricing on alcohol deaths and hospital admissions, such as the Scottish evaluation on the project list (Wyper et al., 2023).

domains.note: A two-page comment with 14 references chosen by the authors; no search or selection criteria.

GBD 2016 is called state-of-the-art and definitive without any appraisal of its weighting, of its interval for the minimum or of its reliance on observational relative risks; the J-curve meta-analyses are set aside in one sentence.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The ranking of policies rests on a single review whose first author is R Burton; the health argument rests on GBD 2016, which is not the authors' work.

A prediction (a dramatic divergence of mortality between Scotland and England within a few years) and value statements (no downsides to limiting marketing; commercial interests ahead of human consequences) are interleaved with evidence and not marked as such.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against a health benefit of low-level drinking
domains.note: The side under-represented is the evidence for lower risk at low intake and the uncertainty around GBD 2016's zero: its significant J-shaped curve for ischaemic heart disease and its 0–0.8 drinks a day interval are not mentioned; possible costs or trade-offs of the recommended policies are not discussed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to commentaries (METHODS §5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used (model card sc_kish_2017), and the overall judgment is no milder than the worst domain. The comment is advocacy accompanying a modelling paper: it restates GBD 2016's numbers correctly (checked against that paper) but adds no evidence, and its title and characterizations ('definitive', 'clear and unambiguous') go beyond what that paper's own interval shows. Citable for how the 'no safe level' reading of GBD 2016 was framed on publication and for the authors' policy argument; not citable for any estimate (use sc_griswold_2018) or as evidence that no level of drinking improves health. A claim resting only on this comment stays at draft (METHODS §5.3, §6.3).

key_findings.finding: The title states that no level of alcohol consumption improves health.

The comment restates GBD 2016's headline figures: alcohol the seventh leading risk factor for deaths and DALYs in 2016, accounting for 2.2% (95% UI 1.5–3.0) of female and 6.8% (5.8–8.0) of male deaths; at ages 15–49 the leading risk factor, with 3.8% (3.2–4.3) of female and 12.2% (10.8–13.6) of male deaths attributable.
key_findings.note: The same paragraph calls alcohol the “leading cause of DALYs” at ages 15–49; GBD 2016 ranks it as the leading risk factor (reporting issue 1).

key_findings.finding: It gives the GBD 2016 minimum-risk level as 0 g of ethanol a week, presented as the level minimising an individual's risk, and explains it by the lower risks estimated in women for ischaemic heart disease and diabetes being cancelled out by cancer risks that rise steadily with intake; it credits the new method with estimating rather than assuming the counterfactual level and with giving a concrete basis for low-risk drinking advice.

It describes the analysis as epidemiology of the most advanced kind that settles the understanding of alcohol-related harm, and names remaining work: unrecorded consumption, drinking patterns and binge drinking (particularly in young people), and harm beyond health and to people other than the drinker.

It calls the conclusions unambiguous: the small gains at low intake are more than offset by higher risks of other harms such as cancer; it takes this as strong support for the UK Chief Medical Officers' guideline (no safe level of consumption) and as a reason to prioritise policies that lower population consumption.

Policy argument: cutting affordability through taxes or price controls such as minimum unit pricing is ranked first for effectiveness and cost-effectiveness, ahead of marketing regulation and limits on availability (citing Burton et al., 2017), and the same measures are likened to tobacco control and to what obesity will need. The authors present Scotland's minimum unit pricing (from May 2018) as a large natural experiment with England as the comparison, and suggest that death and illness rates in the two might draw apart sharply within a few years.

Declarations: both authors employed by Public Health England (RB full-time, NS part-time); NS reports grants from the British Liver Trust and the Alcohol Education Research Council, consultancy and travel expenses from Gilead, paid medicolegal work, and advisory roles on alcohol policy; no funding statement.

reporting_issues.issue: The comment calls alcohol the “leading cause of DALYs” at ages 15–49; GBD 2016 reports it as the leading risk factor for that age group.
reporting_issues.consequence: A risk factor is presented as a cause of disease burden; claims must use GBD 2016's wording.

reporting_issues.issue: The minimum-risk level is restated as 0 g a week with no interval, following GBD 2016's abstract, which itself prints the interval per week rather than per day (see sc_griswold_2018, reporting issue 1).
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers of the comment cannot see that the estimate is compatible with up to 0.8 drinks a day.

reporting_issues.issue: The Scottish policy change is described as a controlled natural experiment, with “England as the placebo control”.
reporting_issues.consequence: A non-randomized comparison between countries is described in the language of a placebo-controlled trial, which overstates what such a comparison can show.

reporting_issues.issue: The phrase attributed to the UK Chief Medical Officers' guideline (“no safe level of alcohol consumption”) is cited to the 2016 report without a page.
reporting_issues.consequence: The quotation was not checked against the guideline in this reading; a claim using it should cite the guideline itself.
